statements.claim: Narakasura, called Bhauma, son of the earth goddess, had grown until his body seemed to fill the heavens and the world cowered in his shadow.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5 (pack excerpt): 'Seeing the son of the earth-goddess who devoured the heavens, he slew him' (Sanskrit: sutaṃ mṛdhe khaṃ vapuṣā grasantaṃ ... dharitryā).

statements.claim: He carried off the princesses of the earth, daughters of kings, and shut them away in his citadel of Pragjyotisha, beyond mountains, water and fire.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.6: 'the princesses seized by Bhauma' (nara-deva-kanyāḥ kujena); Pragjyotisha as Naraka's stronghold and its mountain/fire/water defenses are established in the same cluster (BP 10.59.2-5).

statements.claim: The kings who had tried to win the princesses back had broken themselves against those walls and gone home defeated.
statements.evidence: No specific failed rescue by kings is in the pack; generic amplification of the captivity's hopelessness (cf. Harivamsha 1.121: 'nobody... could take them away').

statements.claim: It was Krishna who finally went against the demon; the son of the earth met the friend of the distressed, and the earth could not save him; the demon was struck down and with his fall the captivity ended.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5-6: Krishna slew the earth-goddess's son; Hari is named 'friend of the distressed' (ārta-bandhum) and the seized princesses, seeing him, rose and chose him.

statements.claim: Seeing Hari, the sixteen thousand princesses came out of their prisons and of their own will chose him, asking to be his.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.6: seeing Hari the friend of the distressed, they rose and chose him (cf. BP 3.3.6 in canto-3 passage: utthāya sadyo jagṛhuḥ).

statements.claim: In one moment, in their many houses, he took their hands - the giving of the hand, the vow of marriage, in every home at the same instant.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.7: 'he took their hands in one moment in their many houses' (āsāṃ muhūrta ekasmin nānāgāreṣu yoṣitām).

statements.claim: In time each of those houses filled with ten sons, children who carried their father's likeness.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.8: 'begetting ten sons in each' (ekaikasyāṃ daśa daśa, per fuller canto-3 passage) and ātma-tulyāni = offspring like himself.

statements.claim: Uddhava remembered and told this afterward to the court of Dwaraka whenever asked about the war in the north.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.5-8 is Uddhava's own narration (excerpt opens 'Uddhava said').

statements.claim: The princesses entered Dwaraka as rescued captives and became the mothers of its future; the city filled with sixteen thousand households.
statements.evidence: Consistent with the maidens being sent to Dvaraka (BP 10.59.35); the forward-looking flourish is framing, not a pack claim.

notes: Recall-bundled story (BP 3.3) fully tracks the pack; all substantive claims supported. 'Sixteen thousand' matches the round canonical count.

statements.claim: Garuda flew to heaven bearing the umbrella of Varuna, the jewel mountain and Krishna on his back, going lightly as if in sport.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30 (Wilson): 'GARUD́A, laden with the umbrella of Varuńa and the jewel mountain, and bearing Hrishikeśa on his back to the court of Indra, went lightly, as if in sport, along.'

statements.claim: At the portals of Swarga Krishna blew his conch and the gods came out to meet him bearing respectful offerings.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'When they arrived at the portals of Swarga, Hari blew his shell; on which the gods advanced to meet him, bearing respectful offerings.'

statements.claim: Aditi, mother of Indra and of the gods, had once kept the earrings that Narakasura had torn away; Krishna bowed before her with Indra beside him, placed the earrings back in her hands and told her the demon was dead.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: Krishna went to 'the palace of the mother of the gods, whose turrets resembled white clouds; and on beholding Adití, paid his respects to her, along with Śakra; and, presenting to her her own earrings, informed her of the destruction of the demon Naraka.'

statements.claim: Aditi's hymn: the lotus-eyed remover of all fear; the eternal, universal, living soul; origin of all beings; evening, night and day; earth, sky, air, water and fire; mind, intellect and individuality; Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva; gods and demons and serpents, men and beasts and trees, the vast and the minute, composed of gathered atoms.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30 hymn, near-verbatim (lotus eyes; removest all fear; eternal, universal, and living soul; origin of all beings; evening, night, day; earth, sky, air, water, fire; mind, intellect, individuality; forms called Brahmá, Vishńu, and Śiva; gods, Daityas, Punnagas, men, animals, trees; all bodies composed of aggregated atoms).

statements.claim: Beyond every perceptible shape is a form no eye can rest on, which she could only glimpse and name; the illusion beguiling those who think 'I am, this is mine' is woven by him, and only worshippers cross it to freedom.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'nor do I know that form of thine, which is beyond perception'; notions 'I am--this is mine' are delusions of the mother of the world originating in his active agency; 'Those men who... diligently worship thee, traverse all this illusion, and obtain spiritual freedom.'

statements.claim: It is a fault to ask small things of one who could give everything - like asking a wish-fulfilling tree for a rag to cover one's nakedness.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'It is the fault of the impure acts of the unrighteous (to proffer such idle requests to one able to confer such more important benefits), like asking for a rag to cover one's nakedness from the tree that bestows whatever is solicited.'

statements.claim: Krishna asked Aditi for her blessing; she granted that while he dwells among mortals, first among men, he shall be invincible to gods and demons alike.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Mother goddess, do thou shew favour unto me, and grant me thy blessing.' ... 'whilst thou dwellest amongst mortals, the first of men, thou shalt be invincible by gods or demons.'

statements.claim: Satyabhama, accompanied by Indra's queen, asked Aditi's blessing and was promised she would never suffer decay nor loss of beauty, becoming the refuge of all loveliness.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Satyabhámá, accompanied by the queen of Indra, addressed Adití... thou shalt never suffer decay, nor loss of beauty: thou shalt be the asylum of all loveliness.'

statements.claim: Indra conducted Krishna and Satyabhama through Nandana and the pleasant gardens of the gods, where the golden Parijata tree that had risen from the churned ocean stood.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'Indra then respectfully saluted Janárddana... and conducted him and Satyabhámá through Nandana and other pleasant gardens of the gods; where Keśava... saw the Párijáta tree... produced when the ocean was churned for ambrosia: the bark was of gold, and it was embellished with young sprouting leaves of a copper colour.'

statements.claim: Far below the clouds, the walls of the demon's citadel still stood, unbroken and waiting.
statements.evidence: No pack support, and it conflicts with the source sequence: the pack passage has Krishna already laden with the umbrella of Varuna and the jewel mountain 'recovered from the demon's hoard' at Pragjyotisha and announcing Naraka's destruction - i.e., Naraka was slain at his stronghold and the hoard recovered BEFORE the earrings reached heaven (cf. VP 5.29-30; BP 10.59.22-37). The line also contradicts this story's own opening ('recovered from the demon's hoard').

corrections.original_sentence: and far below the clouds, in the land of men, the walls of the demon's citadel still stood, unbroken and waiting.
corrections.suggested: and far below the clouds, in the land of men, the demon's conquered city lay still, its stolen hoard already scattered back toward its owners.

notes: Body of the story is near-verbatim VP 5.30 (hymn, blessings, gardens). One issue: the closing transition line asserts the citadel of Pragjyotisha was still standing at the time of the heaven visit, but the earrings were recovered from that citadel after Naraka's fall - the war was already over when they were returned to Aditi.

statements.claim: Narakasura broke into the hoard of heaven, carrying off Varuna's umbrella, Aditi's earrings and the jewel mountain Amara, and the gods could not recover them; Indra came to Krishna with his complaint.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.1-5 (pack excerpt): 'Indra, robbed of his umbrella, earrings and the Amara hill, complained to Krishna.'

statements.claim: Krishna did not summon an army; he took Satyabhama with him, mounted Garuda and went to Pragjyotisha himself.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.2: 'sa-bhāryo garuḍārūḍhaḥ prāg-jyotiṣa-puraṃ yayau' (with his wife, mounted on Garuda, he went to the city of Pragjyotisha).

statements.claim: Pragjyotisha was ringed with mountains, weapon-forts, belts of fire and water, and the snares of Mura, so that nothing that came near ever came back out.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.3-5 rendering names the mountain, weapon-fort, fire/water and Mura-pasha defenses; 'nothing came back out' is hyperbole consistent with the defenses never having been breached.

statements.claim: Krishna broke the mountains with his mace and took the weapon-forts with arrows.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.3: 'gadayā nirbibhedādrīn śastra-durgāṇi sāyakaiḥ' (he split the mountains with his mace, the weapon-forts with arrows).

statements.claim: He cut the fire and water with his discus and severed the snares of Mura with his sword.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59 (pack rendering): 'the fire and water with his discus, and Mura's nooses with his sword.'

statements.claim: The sound of the conch Panchajanya broke the great engines of the city and the hearts of the proud men who served them, terrible as the thunder that ends an age.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.4-5: 'śaṅkha-nādena yantrāṇi hṛdayāni manasvinām' and 'pāñcajanya-dhvaniṃ śrutvā yugāntaśani-bhīṣaṇam' (by the conch-sound the machines and the hearts of the proud; the Panchajanya sound terrible as the end-of-age thunderbolt).

statements.claim: By the time Krishna and Satyabhama reached the inner walls, nothing stood between them and the citadel but one defender rising from the girdling waters.
statements.evidence: Bridge to the Mura episode; BP 10.59.5 has Mura hearing the conch, and BP 10.59.7 has him rising from the waters with five heads.

notes: Defense-by-defense breach maps exactly to BP 10.59.1-5 (mace/mountains, arrows/weapon-forts, discus/fire-water, sword/nooses, conch/engines+hearts). No issues.

statements.claim: Mura, the last guardian, heard the conch and rose from the depths of the waters girdling the citadel.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.5: 'pāñcajanya-dhvaniṃ śrutvā' (having heard the sound of Panchajanya); BP 10.59.7-10 has Mura rising from the waters (papātāmbhasi) - pack rendering: 'Mura, roused by Krishna's conch, rose from the waters.'

statements.claim: Mura had five heads, all of which roared at once, blazing like the fire of the end of the ages and harsh as the sun of the world's last day.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.6-7: 'yugānta-sūryānala-rocir ulbaṇaḥ' (blazing with the fire of the end-of-age sun) and 'vyanadat sa pañcabhiḥ' (he roared with five mouths).

statements.claim: He hurled his trident, so fierce no eye could rest on it, and Krishna broke it in mid-air with two arrows, the three-pronged weapon splitting apart.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.6-8: the trident 'su-durnirīkṣaṇaḥ' (very hard to look at); 'hariḥ śarābhyām abhinat tri-dhojasā' - Krishna split the trident with two arrows (pack rendering: 'Krishna shattered it with two arrows').

statements.claim: Mura's mace came next and Krishna shattered it into a thousand splinters.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.9: 'gadāṃ mṛdhe gadāgrajo nirbibhide sahasradhā' (he shattered the mace into a thousand pieces).

statements.claim: Krishna's discus cut off Mura's five heads, and he fell lifeless into the waters like a mountain whose peaks have been struck off by Indra's thunderbolt.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.10: 'vyasuḥ papātāmbhasi kṛtta-śīrṣo nikṛtta-śṛṅgo 'drir ivendra-tejasā' (lifeless he fell into the water, head cut off, like a mountain with peaks struck off by Indra's power).

statements.claim: Mura had seven sons - Tamra, Antariksha, Sravana, Vibhavasu, Vasu, Nabhasvan and Aruna - who came out armed to avenge their father and flung themselves at Krishna.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.11-12: the seven names appear verbatim (tāmro 'ntarikṣaḥ śravaṇo vibhāvasur vasur nabhasvān aruṇaś ca saptamaḥ); pack rendering: 'slew Mura's seven sons who attacked to avenge their father'; verse 12 lists their arrows, swords, maces, śaktis, ṛṣṭis and tridents.

statements.claim: Krishna brought all seven down, cutting through arms and armor, until all seven lay with Mura before the citadel.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.13: 'tān pīṭha-mukhyān anayad yama-kṣayaṃ nikṛtta-śīrṣoru-bhujāṅghri-varmaṇaḥ' (he sent them to Yama's abode, heads, thighs, arms and armor cut off).

statements.claim: From the citadel heights Narakasura watched Krishna on Garuda with Satyabhama, blazing like a storm cloud crowned with lightning above the sun, and hurled the sataghni (hundred-killer) while all his warriors loosed their shafts.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.14: 'dṛṣṭvā sa-bhāryaṃ garuḍopari sthitaṃ sūryopariṣṭāt sa-taḍid ghanaṃ yathā... vyasṛjac chata-ghnīṃ' (seeing him with his wife atop Garuda, above the sun, like a cloud with lightning, he released the sataghni); 'yodhāś ca sarve yugapac ca vivyadhuḥ' (all his warriors struck simultaneously).

statements.claim: When the air cleared the rider was still there, unharmed.
statements.evidence: Not stated in the quoted verses, but consistent with Naraka's defeat in the immediately following episode (BP 10.59, next corpus story 'Krishna Slays Narakasura').

notes: Sequence and details (trident broken by two arrows, mace shattered, discus beheading, seven sons' names, sataghni) match BP 10.59.5-14 exactly. No issues.

statements.claim: In the aftermath, Narakasura, the son of the earth who had harried the gods and hoarded the treasures of heaven, lay dead in his fortress city of Pragjyotisha.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.22 opens with the earth goddess approaching Krishna after the slaying; Naraka's death, thefts and hoard are the established cluster facts (previous corpus story: 'Krishna Slays Narakasura').

statements.claim: Bhumi, the goddess of the earth, came before Krishna, the slayer of her son.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.22-23: 'tataś ca bhūḥ kṛṣṇam upetya' (then Earth approached Krishna); Bhumi is Naraka's mother (Bhauma = son of the earth).

statements.claim: In her hands she carried Aditi's earrings blazing with refined gold and precious stones, Varuna's great umbrella, and the great jewel, and gave them back.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.22: 'kuṇḍale pratapta-jāmbūnada-ratna-bhāsvare... prācetasaṃ chatram atho mahā-maṇim' (the earrings blazing with refined gold and jewels, the umbrella of Varuna [son of Pracetas] and the great jewel).

statements.claim: She praised Krishna: homage to the lotus-navelled one, wearer of the garland of lotuses; to Vasudeva, Vishnu, the unborn creator of endless power; who bears the great darkness for its destruction and is not touched by it; who upholds goodness; who is time, primal matter and the supreme person.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.24-28: 'namaḥ paṅkaja-nābhāya namaḥ paṅkaja-māline... vāsudevāya viṣṇave... ajāya janayitre 'sya brahmaṇe 'nanta-śaktaye... tamo nirodhāya bibharṣy asaṃvṛtaḥ... kālaḥ pradhānaṃ puruṣo bhavān paraḥ.'

statements.claim: She counted herself among his works: 'I am the water, the fire, the wind, the sky; the elements, the gods, the mind, the senses.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.29: 'ahaṃ payo jyotir athānilo nabho mātrāṇi devā mana indriyāṇi.'

statements.claim: The purpose of her visit was her frightened son Bhagadatta (son of Naraka), who had come for refuge at Krishna's lotus feet, and Krishna granted him fearlessness.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.30-31: 'tasyātmajo 'yaṃ tava pāda-paṅkajaṃ bhītaḥ prapannārti-haropasāditaḥ' (this son of his, frightened, has approached your lotus feet, O remover of the affliction of the surrendered); pack excerpt: 'begged Krishna to protect her son Bhagadatta; Krishna granted him fearlessness.' Bhagadatta as Naraka's son matches BP 3.3.5, where the kingdom is given to Naraka's son after the slaying.

statements.claim: The treasures of heaven were free of the demon's vault; the earrings of Aditi would travel onward to be returned in the courts of heaven, and a new king sat on Naraka's throne, placed there by mercy.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.37 has Krishna restore the earrings to Aditi in Indra's abode after this scene; BP 3.3.5: after slaying Naraka, Krishna gave the remainder (the kingdom) to Naraka's son (āmantritas tat-tanayāya śeṣaṃ dattvā).

statements.claim: The city watched in silence as its master's body was borne away; Bhumi did not weep for Naraka nor ask vengeance.
statements.evidence: Atmosphere/framing; the pack records Bhumi's prayer for Bhagadatta but no grief or vengeance plea - the framing does not contradict it.

notes: Bhumi's offering (earrings/umbrella/great jewel), her hymn and the plea for Bhagadatta with the grant of fearlessness all track BP 10.59.22-31. The story's genealogy (Bhagadatta = Naraka's son, Bhumi = his mother) is the standard one and matches BP 3.3.5; the pack excerpt's loose 'her son Bhagadatta' is not followed as the primary reading. No issues.

statements.claim: In Naraka's treasury were diamonds, pearls, corals, sapphires and emeralds, heaps of gold and jewels gathered from gods, gandharvas and serpents, a bed shining like the moon, a lion-shaped throne bright as burning fire, and Varuna's great umbrella, cloud-colored and moon-lustered with a standard of gold.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'diamonds, pearls, corals, sapphires, emeralds... a highly costly bed shining like the moon, a lion-shaped throne effulgent like burning fire, and a huge and beautiful umbrella of the hue of the clouds of the rainy season, of the lustre of the moon and with a golden standard'; jewels formerly with 'the gods, Gandharvas and Pannagas (serpents).'

statements.claim: Krishna took the great umbrella of Varuna for himself, as his share of the hoard.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'Taking himself the Varuni umbrella capable of showering gold, he rode Garuda.'

statements.claim: In the inner chambers Naraka had shut away 16,100 royal princesses, daughters of kings seized from their families; seeing Krishna they were captivated, and in that first glance each mentally chose him: 'May this man be my husband; may the creator ratify my choice.'
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.32-34: 'rājanya-kanyānāṃ... striyo vīkṣya nara-varyaṃ vimohitāḥ... bhūyāt patir ayaṃ mahyaṃ dhātā tad anumodatām' (pack rendering: 16,100 royal princesses; seeing him they were enchanted; 'may this man be my husband, may the creator ratify my choice').

statements.claim: They came to him thin from fasting and vows, wearing the single braid of a woman whose husband is absent, dressed in silk, with folded hands, standing around him without fear because word of Naraka's death had reached them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'emaciated on account of the observance of vows and fastings, clad in silken raiments and with one braid of hairs approached Janarddana with folded hands and stood encircling him. They fearlessly surrounded Krishna because they had learnt of the death of the great Asuras.'

statements.claim: They had lived in the seraglio deprived of every enjoyment yet unharmed, like celestial maidens lodged in a city of the gods, and the elder guardians of the palace bowed to Krishna as he passed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'Although deprived of all sorts of enjoyments, still residing there as if in the city of the celestials, they lived happily like celestial damsels... The elderly Mānavas who were their guards... bowed to Krishna.'

statements.claim: They told him that the sage Narada and the wind-god had long ago promised that Narayana himself would slay Naraka and become their husband.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'What the celestial saint Nārada... and the Wind-god had said to us before... They said that the Universal Lord Nārāyana... slaying Bhumi's son Naraka, would in no time become our husband.'

statements.claim: Krishna consoled them and sent the treasures ahead to Dwaraka - Naraka's twenty thousand war elephants carrying bows and lances, forty thousand she-elephants and eight hundred thousand horses - while sixty-four four-tusked white elephants of the breed of Airavata bore the maidens and their wealth toward Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'twenty thousand grim-visaged elephants carrying bows, Tomaras... forty-thousand she-elephants, and eight lacs of horses'; BP 10.59.35-36: Krishna sent the maidens to Dvaraka with 'airāvata-kulebhāṃś ca catur-dantāṃs tarasvinaḥ' (pack rendering: sixty-four white elephants of Airavata's breed, four-tusked and swift).

statements.claim: In Dwaraka the news stirred the streets: 16,100 royal brides were on the road and the riches of a demon king were arriving.
statements.evidence: Framing of the aftermath; consistent with the maidens and treasures being sent to Dvaraka ahead of Krishna.

notes: Follows BP 10.59.31-36 with Harivamsha 1.121 corroboration (treasury inventory, maiden's description, Narada/wind-god prophecy, elephant/horse counts). The tradition note correctly acknowledges the Harivamsha's Mount Mani variant while following the BP location. No issues.

statements.claim: Krishna came up to Indra's heaven carrying Aditi's earrings, which the demon Naraka had torn from her; Indra and the gods received him with worship, and Aditi, pleased, took back what was hers.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.37: 'gatvā surendra-bhavanaṃ dattvādityai ca kuṇḍale' (going to Indra's abode, he gave Aditi the earrings); Harivamsha 1.121: 'Giving to the king of gods the pair of ear-rings belonging to Aditi... Aditi was pleased.'

statements.claim: Satyabhama had seen the Parijata tree, the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods, and wanted it for her own garden in Dwaraka; wishing to please his beloved like an ordinary man, the Lord went for the celestial tree.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.4: 'priyaṃ prabhur grāmya iva priyāyā vidhitsur ārcchad dyutaruṃ' (the Lord, like a common man, desiring to please his beloved, went for the celestial tree); BP 10.59.38: 'codito bhāryayotpāṭya pārījātaṃ garutmati' (urged by his wife, he uprooted the Parijata onto Garuda).

statements.claim: The ruler of the universe uprooted the tree from the middle of heaven, whole, roots and all, and set it on Garuda.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.121: 'Krishna of unlimited powers, forcibly up-rooted it and placed it on Garuda's head'; Harivamsha 1.220: 'uprooted the Pārijāta tree and placed it on the back of Garuda'; BP 10.59.38.

statements.claim: Shachi protested that the tree belonged to her; it was not proper, Govinda, to remove it.
statements.evidence: VP 5.30: 'This Párijáta tree belongs to Śachí... it is not proper, Govinda, for you to remove it.'

statements.claim: Indra, blind with rage, rushed at Krishna with all his host, as though Krishna were a plaything of the women; Krishna turned aside the thunderbolt and defeated host after host of the immortals.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.4: 'vajry ādravat taṃ sa-gaṇo ruṣāndhaḥ krīḍā-mṛgo nūnam ayaṃ vadhūnām' (the thunderbolt-wielder rushed at him with his host, blind with rage: 'surely this is a plaything of the women'); BP 10.59.37-40 rendering: 'overcame Indra and the gods'; VP 5.31 has Krishna return Indra's cast thunderbolt.

statements.claim: In the end Indra let the Parijata go, and the wish-fulfilling tree of heaven was given to the earth.
statements.evidence: VP 5.31 (Indra consents: 'Let this Párijáta tree be transferred to Dwáraká'); BP 10.59.39 has it planted in Satyabhama's garden.

statements.claim: Over Dwaraka Krishna blew his conch and the whole city rose at the sound; he planted the Parijata in Satyabhama's garden, where it perfumed the earth for three furlongs, let those who approached recall past lives, and showed the Yadavas their original celestial forms.
statements.evidence: VP 5.31: 'he blew his shell, and delighted all the inhabitants... planted the great Párijáta tree, the smell of which perfumed the earth for three furlongs, and an approach to which enabled every one to recollect the events of a prior existence; so that... all the Yádavas contemplated themselves in their (original) celestial forms.'

statements.claim: Uddhava remembered the episode later with wonder - the lord, wishing to please his beloved like a common man, carrying the celestial tree home for his wife.
statements.evidence: BP 3.3.4 is Uddhava's own recall of exactly this episode (priyaṃ prabhur grāmya iva priyāyā...).

notes: All beats (earrings restoration, Satyabhama's wish, uprooting, Shachi's protest, Indra's attack and defeat, planting in Satyabhama's garden with its three-furlong perfume and past-life recall) supported by BP 10.59.37-40, BP 3.3.4, HV 1.121/1.220 and VP 5.30-31. No issues.

statements.claim: In Dwaraka 16,100 brides were waiting - the maidens Krishna had freed from Naraka's palace, princesses, daughters of kings from many lands, who had come to the city with the demon's treasures.
statements.evidence: VP 5.31: 'the wealth, elephants, horses, and women, which he had recovered from Naraka... brought to Dwáraká by the servants of the demon'; count 'Sixteen thousand and one hundred' per VP 5.31 and BP 10.59.32.

statements.claim: They had chosen him with their own eyes the moment they saw him standing in the demon's hall, before a word was spoken.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.33-34: seeing him the women were captivated and each wished 'may this man be my husband.'

statements.claim: Krishna took possession of the wealth, the elephants and the horses recovered from Naraka.
statements.evidence: VP 5.31: 'Then Krishńa took possession of the wealth, elephants, horses, and women, which he had recovered from Naraka.'

statements.claim: At an auspicious season the wedding came; in separate mansions across Dwaraka, in a single moment, Krishna multiplied himself into as many forms and received the hand of every one of the 16,100 brides according to the ritual, each bride believing he was hers alone.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.41: 'muhūrta ekasmin nānāgāreṣu' (in a single moment, in separate mansions); VP 5.31: 'at an auspicious season he espoused all the maidens... at one and the same moment he received the hands of all of them, according to the ritual, in separate mansions. Sixteen thousand and one hundred was the number... into so many different forms did the foe of Madhu multiply himself; so that every one of the damsels thought that he had wedded her in his single person.'

statements.claim: Krishna took up residence in each of those houses, living with each wife as a householder, undivided, in a way beyond all reckoning and comparison; none but the Lord could perform such a feat.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.42: 'gṛheṣu tāsām anapāyy atarka-kṛn nirasta-sāmyātiśayeṣv avasthitaḥ' (he dwelt in their homes, never absent, unthinkable, beyond all comparison); VP 5.31: 'the creator of the world, Hari... abode severally in the dwelling of each of these his wives.'

statements.claim: Even Brahma and the other gods cannot trace his path - cannot follow how one man is wholly present to 16,100 wives.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.43: 'brahmādayo 'pi na viduḥ padavīṃ yadīyām' (even Brahma and the others do not know his path).

statements.claim: The brides rose to greet him and offered seats; they worshipped him, washed his feet, brought betel, rest, cooling fans, garlands and perfumes, and tended his hair, bed and bath; hundreds of maidservants served each household, and their love only grew.
statements.evidence: BP 10.59.44: 'pratyudgamāsana-varārhaṇa-pada-śauca-tāmbūla-viśramaṇa-vījana-gandha-mālyaiḥ keśa-prasāra-śayana-snapanopahāryaiḥ dāsī-śatā api vibhor vidadhuḥ sma dāsyam' (rising, seats, worship, foot-washing, betel, rest, fanning, perfumes, garlands, hair-dressing, beds, baths - even hundreds of maidservants served the Lord); v.43: their love grew ceaselessly (edhitayānurāga).

statements.claim: Each marriage was complete: each bride had her husband fully, not a fraction of him divided among thousands - a king might marry many wives by proxy, but this was different.
statements.evidence: Theological reflection consistent with the text's insistence on Krishna's undivided, simultaneous presence (BP 10.59.42-43); the proxy-marriage contrast is the narrator's framing, not a pack claim.

notes: The simultaneous mass wedding, the multiplication into as many forms, residence in every house, Brahma's inability to trace his path, and the wives' loving service all track BP 10.59.41-44 and VP 5.31. No issues.
